utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Yes. I did understand, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that you have provided additional copies of the "determination de la Defense avec la Chambre aux temoins employes du bureau du procureur Monsieur Philips et Lesic." I also understood that it has been filed this morning, but the Chamber has not yet had an opportunity to read it. It is not on our desks yet. So we will do it as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I provided a copy of the document to the Prosecution so they know of it. Also, as soon as it was possible, we faxed the document and last night we also sent another document stating that since we were not able to copy the transcript, we needed a few more hours in order to inform you about our position. Even though we were talking about Rule 94 bis, we could have asked for the deadline to be respected, but we did it in this way and that also applies to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I think we first now turn into closed session in order to hear the answer from Ms. Pilipovic on a question that has been put to the Defence by the Chamber. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before that, I don't know if I have already said that, but I was asked to mention for the transcript the fact that we gave to the Registry a translation of Exhibit D85, that was a document that hasn't been dealt with yet. But we did talk about it yesterday. So this document should now be in the hands of the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I -- I take it that the Defence has been prepared by the Tribunal and, therefore I do not expect any problems from the Prosecution in respect of this translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have an opportunity to look through it. I don't expect there to be any problem, but we will apprise the Court if there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it is more practical to do it the other way. There was the document D85 was provisionally admitted because there was no translation. There is a translation now. Therefore, we admitted the document, but of course, if there is any specific issue arising from this translation, the Prosecution always can address the Chamber and ask to reconsider its decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then D85 is admitted into evidence. And apart from D85, then now the translation of that same document is D85.1 is admitted into evidence as well. May we then turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we will ask the usher to bring in the witness, I first would like to give already orally the decision on the request of the Prosecution to add Mr. Hogan to the list of witnesses and to have his statement admitted into evidence under Rule 92 bis. The request is denied and you will receive a written decision, I hope, by tomorrow. But I already can give you in short, the reasons why. There are two elements in the statement. Neither of these elements -- one is an explanation of the efforts taken by the Prosecution to find and analyse UNPROFOR reports, and the second part is measurements on sniping incident locations. It's -- the Chamber is of the opinion that the interest of justice do not demand at this moment adding the name of Mr. Hogan to the witness list, and apart from that, the relevance that it would add to the evidence already presented in this court, the statement of Mr. Hogan is not such that under Rule 92 bis, we think we should use our discretionary power to admit this evidence. That is in short our decision, but you will get it in detail in a written decision. I expect as well, either this afternoon or tomorrow, that the decision on 92 bis on all the other statements will be filed so that it is accessible to both parties. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. President. Just before the witness is recalled, do you have in mind a time or a stage of the hearing today when we will return to the issue of the recalling of Zoran Lesic and Richard Philipps? I will be present to suit the Trial Chamber's convenience in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you yet, because we have not seen and we have not read what the Defence has written. So, therefore, we will first, during the first break, I take it that the Chamber will read at least the response and then consider whether we could deal with it today or only in the beginning of next week -- tomorrow or the beginning of next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have just received the French copy ourselves, but I anticipate I will be ready at the beginning of the next session, should you be ready. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will inform Mr. Stamp so that he can call you. Meanwhile I see that the addendum to the report of Ewa Tabeau has been handed over to the Chamber. I take it that -- no, you have not yet received it. It will be given to the parties and in due course, the parties will be given the opportunity to put additional questions to Ewa Tabeau, but only in respect of this addendum. Then, Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Hadzic. I again remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you may resume the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague has three or four questions and then I will finish the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just to check about the time, we were informed that we still have an hour, so did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yesterday I believe you told us one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think I said half an hour, at least that is what the Registrar told me and I then checked it when she did write down her calculation. And I had to agree with her it was half an hour. But if we together made a mistake, then you would please come and tell us exactly how you would have calculated more than one half hour left at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Pilipovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, during the examination-in-chief and also during cross-examination by the Defence, you said that you had good relations with UNPROFOR. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were commander, and I am talking about the period in 1992, 1993, and 1994 were there any incidents with members of UNPROFOR in the sense that they were physically mistreated or that they were shot at by members of the 5th Brigade? Were there any incidents like that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did you have meets with the members of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the French Battalion, which was stationed at the airport, we had meetings every week.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to show the witness a document. It is document D163.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you have a document before you? From the 5th of December, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the right-hand corner it is signed by Commander of the Headquarters of the Supreme Command, Delic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Below the date, the 5th of December, 1993, it is noted that an inquiry was conducted about the wounding of an UN member in the settlement of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At our intervention, I repeat, we asked the general staff to launch this investigation in order to establish who shot the French soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, does it say in line two of this document, since the authorised UN committee did conduct an investigation about the wounding of Legionnaire Petkov --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note, we don't have a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- who is part of the UN forces, the result of the inquiry notes that the soldier was wounded from a building which was in the zone controlled by members.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence believes that perhaps we did give this document to the interpreters. Perhaps, they didn't receive one by mistake, but I do have a copy for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hadzic, this document, does it indicate that a member of the UN was wounded in a zone which was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wounded, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your term in office, did you have contact with Mr. Stjepan Siber?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stjepan Siber was in the General Staff and during the war, he visited me only once when I left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, are you aware that Mr. Siber has written a war diary?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, if I were to tell you that Mr. Siber in his diary, under the date of the 15th of July 1992 wrote that in conversation -- in a conversation which he had that day, Colonel Jones also participated, and he asked him for snipers from Dobrinja not to fire at them. Can you answer us, from which positions did the snipers of the 5th Motorised Brigade fire at the members of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question has in it a component which assumes that the witness has accepted that snipers of the 5th Motorised Brigade did fire at members of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please clarify the underlying issue, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, did members of UNPROFOR, while you were commander of the 5th Motorised Brigade, protest to you about snipers from the 5th Motorised Brigade firing at UNPROFOR members?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, if I were to tell you that Mr. Stjepan Siber, in his diary, wrote that a member of UNPROFOR was lodging a protest because snipers from Dobrinja were firing at members of UNPROFOR, would you agree with me that this is correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I repeat no. Because we controlled the entire area of Dobrinja and -- we did not control the entire territory of Dobrinja and Serb snipers fired from Dobrinja I and perhaps they were the one who hit the French UNPROFOR members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Siber says that this -- the French UNPROFOR protested to him saying that snipers from the 5th Motorised Brigade, from that zone, were firing on UNPROFOR members.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please explain to me who Mr. Jones is?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I stated that Mr. Siber, in his diary, wrote that on the 15th of July, 1992, Mr. Colonel Jones, a member of UNPROFOR, lodged a protest with Mr. Siber because snipers from Dobrinja were firing at members of UNPROFOR, thinking of snipers from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So those from the 5th Motorised Brigade. So if Mr. Siber published this in his diary, would you agree with me that this correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, this is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I -- there seems to be quite some confusion. Are you asking whether the complaint by Mr. Jones was justified because the facts upon which it was based were true; or are you asking whether it is true that there was a complaint? Which is, of course, something different. I repeatedly heard you put the question to the witness which is not very clear, and then -- or at least if you take it literally, it is about whether it is true that there was a complaint. And I hear the witness answering again and again about the underlying facts. Could you please clarify that there is no further mistake -- no further confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before my friend continues, may I just observe that she is questioning the witness about something which she has not shown him but she quotes from the book and having regard from the documents that we have been delivered has been quoted incorrectly from the book. In that she said that somebody in a war diary wrote that members of the 5th Motorised Brigade were firing at UNPROFOR members. From a document that we have had from the Defence, we do not see that there. So if she is going to quote from the book, we ask her to quote accurately, firstly, and secondly, perhaps it is better if she is going to ask about the writings of somebody, to let him have a look at the writings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, the Chamber did not check the correctness of the quote --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... but would you please do it or give the text too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you have a document before you where it states on the first page, "Deceits, Falsehoods and Truth" and this is written by Stjepan Siber?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that document have a page 108?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it a copy -- is the copy that is in front of you, does that copy have page 108?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I will quote to you, paragraph two, on page 108, where Mr. Siber states --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, paragraph, "the discussion was then joined by Colonel Jones," this is written by Mr. Siber, "and he asked for us snipers from Dobrinja not to fire at them and then I answered, 'Mr. Colonel, whoever is firing at you, you should fire at them back because that person was not ordered to do this by anyone.'" Mr. Hadzic, did Mr. Siber, either verbally, or in writing, tell you about the protest by -- the protest by Colonel Jones about snipers from Dobrinja firing at UNPROFOR members in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I am reiterating, we did not control the entire Dobrinja. The BH Army never fired at soldiers from the mission, soldiers who were honorably carrying out their duty at Sarajevo airport. And they were helping us so that we could survive in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, a couple of minutes ago, we had a document -- you had a document before you from which it could be concluded that an UN member had been injured in the area of responsibility of the BH Army as he was unloading a humanitarian aid convoy. So what is the truth?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth, the only truth is that we did not fire at these people and we asked ballistic investigation, our investigation from the Main Staff, from the 1st Corps, in order to find out who fired at these people, at this person, who was bringing humanitarian aid to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, bearing in mind your first answer, you said that members of the 5th Motorised Brigade never fired at UN members and bearing in mind the document that you were given by the Defence, which is the document of the BH Army, also bearing in mind what Mr. Siber says about UN protest about snipers in Dobrinja firing at UNPROFOR members, would you agree with me that having looked at these documents, you are not telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam before this honourable Court, I swore that I would tell the truth. I cannot tell falsehoods. I am reiterating, never have our people from the 5th Motorised Brigade fired at UNPROFOR members. The document you have shown me from the General Staff does not confirm it. This is our own request. We wanted to have this investigated because the UNPROFOR never managed to investigate this, never wanted to establish this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, at my question, whether members of the 5th Motorised Brigade fired at UN members you said no?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, in 1995 you were removed from the post of the commander of the 5th Motorised Brigade by the commander of the 1st Corps, Mr. Karavelic. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us why were you replaced?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was replaced because I had dismissed 200 people from the manpower of the 5th Motorised Brigade, 200 people who were not able to carry out military service, either because of their age, because they were using drugs or because they were sick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, while you were a commander, specifically, we are talking about 1992, 1993, and 1994, did you personally have complaints from the command of the 1st Corps about your work?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there had been complaints, people would have replaced me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to show the document D165.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. I don't want to interfere, but you said three or four questions. You took 20 minutes now, approximately, of the half hour remaining.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, can you see the document which on the left corner bears the date of the 7th of December, 1993? From the document you can see that the document was delivered to the command of the 1st Corps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document has not -- doesn't have a seal anywhere. So, a certification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am just asking you whether this document is a report on the problem of command and control in the 5th Motorised Brigade to be delivered to the commander of the 1st Corps. I am just asking whether this is what it says in the document in the first line.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, in the penultimate line of this document, seventh line from the bottom, it says "he is behaving in an autocratic manner, provoking argument. He is not carrying out duties from the authority of the commander because he is only receiving people in his office, and only those people who are going through Dobrinja i.e. through the tunnel." From this document, may one conclude that you have had problems with the command of the 1st Corps and that these reports, such reports, were delivered to the command of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it cannot be concluded from this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that you were never called for talks at the command of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of this document, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you call for talks because in Dobrinja you wished to establish Muslim armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I never tried to do that, ever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you know about the prison called "Sunce" or "Sun," which is in the area of Dobrinja under the control of the 5th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a facility was never under the control of the 5th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, if I put it to you that people who were in the camp in the facility called Sunce, a report was filed to the Prosecutor's office of the International Tribunal against you, a person who was in charge of detaining people, only Serbs, in the prison Sunce. Could you perhaps answer this question, whether you have any such knowledge of these things?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I put it to you that there are people who have filed such a report, have submitted such report, and who were in this prison in 1992, 1993, and 1994, would you agree with me that this is correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, the Dobrinja Brigade had, as part of its composition, military detention which was only for the members of the 5th Motorised Brigade for breaking discipline. And this facility that you have mentioned under this name was never under the control of the Dobrinja Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge whether this facility existed and it was under the control of the special police or of the battalion of the Military Police, under the control of the Mr. Kerim Loncarevic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that from the 5th or the 6th -- the 5th of July, from which brigade was founded, we did not have this facility, we did not control it. From the 6th of July, from the moment that the Dobrinja Brigade existed as formation of the 1st Corps, we did not have such a facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence would now like to ask Mr. Piletta-Zanin to continue cross-examination, who has got a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President may I just say that we have had a problem in the calculation in the time left over by something that you had said: [In English] "An hour left."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have checked it the transcript and that is what the transcript says and it also says clearly that the Prosecution took two and a half hours. It is my recollection that I said half an hour, but I might make a mistake, I am not quite sure, but I repeatedly said that the Prosecution took two and a half hours. I will grant you 10 more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated, page 13, line 14, a moment ago, you said that nobody had fired on UN forces. How can you be certain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please -- I didn't think that that is what the witness said, Mr. Piletta-Zanin: "Nobody had fired on UN forces." At least, from the context, it must have been certain that the witness testified that none of, may I say it, his troops or those belonging to his troops fired at UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that nobody from the 5th Brigade had ever fired on the troops of the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could you be absolutely certain of this and not allow the possibility that any of your men may have taken a spontaneous decision to fire?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that the cooperation that we had with the French Battalion which was based in Dobrinja, it was very good cooperation. Once a week we had meetings, and if such a thing had happened, these people would have told me about the problem. They never told us about this. At these meetings, they did not warn us that anyone was firing from our side on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, my question is the following: Could you, today, under oath, completely rule out the possibility that one of your people had ever opened fire on UN forces? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, today, under oath, could you completely rule out the possibility that one of your people, perhaps even without orders, had ordered -- had fired on UN forces? Could you please answer with a "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I thought that my question was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is, Mr. Hadzic, whether you think it would be totally impossible that someone of your troops, perhaps without you knowing it or not anything being reported to you, might have fired once on someone of the UNPROFOR forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what you said, that is possible. It is possible that somebody had fired and I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, this is your answer. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the tunnel from Dobrinja to Butmir was officially opened on the 30th of July. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, before the official opening of the tunnel, was this tunnel in operation?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if the official opening of the tunnel occurred on the 30th of July, could we consider that, a few days before the official opening, the tunnel had indeed been broken through?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was linked and it was open on the 30th of July, 1992. And after the breakthrough or the linkage from one to the other side, the first units of the BH army then left Sarajevo and went out to Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just for the record, there is a matter of translation which I think is important. I think the date should be the 30th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it says 1992, but that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, a little before the official opening of the tunnel, the people were still working on the tunnel, right? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even after the opening, the people were still working on the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. These people were soldiers; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were soldiers. From our brigade, people who worked there, they were soldiers, and also people from other brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. There was no Serb who was forced to work there; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? I don't find it very clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no Serb worker there who was forced to work on the tunnel; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who worked there were from our brigade. They were all volunteers to work on the tunnel. There were 71 of them. Out of that, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there were 15 who were non-Bosniaks, and the rest were Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just ask you do answer very briefly, this tunnel, from July 1993, did it allow you to bring in weapons? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To start with, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. This tunnel did it allow you to bring in or bring out forces?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no forces that were brought in, but there were people -- there were forces that were brought out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this tunnel was a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. Because -- because through the tunnel, civilians and soldiers went through it. That was the only communication between Sarajevo and the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, you spoke in your statement about the army in that it did not go to certain -- did not go to get supply water from certain stations because it had tanks, water systems, water tanks that were mobile. Is that correct; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your statement that you were getting your water from the brewery. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, was this a brewery that was located in the area of Bistrik or in another area?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the area of Bistrik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, was there just a brewery there in Bistrik, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is only one brewery in Bistrik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if in this area, and in this brewery, wasn't there a workshop for making -- for manufacturing weapons? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, these mobile cisterns, were these cisterns towed by civilian vehicles? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were driven by a soldier. These water cisterns that you talked about, were they towed, that is, were they towed by civilian vehicles or at least did they seem to be towed by civilian vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a motor vehicle with a tank towing a cistern attached and the driver was a member of the brigade. We received the cistern from the utility company and they used those cisterns in order to wash the streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, do you know if vehicles like front-loading lorries could be used by the army for identical needs, that is, in order to dig and in order to use as excavators?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I am just going to confer, Mr. President, for 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, this is our last question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you have already gone 12-13 minutes. Last question now, means last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The very last one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to give you the following dates three dates: 1st of June 1993, 12th of July 1993, and 4th of February 1994. Are you certain that there was no combat on these dates that I have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Re-examined by Mr. Stamp:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect to the last question you were asked by the Defence, you said, as far as you know, there was no combat on three dates that you were given. You are in a position, I take it, to speak about your brigade's area of responsibility; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you indicated that a JNA that occupied Mojmilo hill were eventually designated by you as a Serb army, and you said: "Serbs arrived and changed the flag." The Serbs changed the flag from what flag to what flag?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the soldiers just reached the Mojmilo hill, it was the JNA with the Yugoslav flag. After the Albanian members of the JNA fled from Mojmilo, the composition changed. The Serb army came and they hoisted the Serbian flag in that place. There was no longer the Yugoslav flag flying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these regular Serb army soldiers that hoisted these flags, the Serb flags?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were members of the reserves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in cross-examination that in the early months of 1992, a large number of Serbs left Dobrinja. You also said before that in response to me that approximately 30 per cent of the personnel in your brigade, and I should say approximately 13, 1-3 per cent of the personnel in your brigade, were Serbs. Among the civilians, did all the Serb civilians leave Dobrinja or did some remain and continue living there during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all left Dobrinja. A lot of Serbs remained to live there. The most precise data is the data from the Red Cross, that is in possession of the civilian protection, civil protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there was a period of time when you had problems with a Military Police unit. Did -- was any action ever taken to resolve these problems or could you tell us what became of that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the structuring of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this problem was resolved, and the person who was commanding that police unit was replaced. And that formation that he headed was disbanded and the people were re-allocated to other brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were shown a document marked D160 and I ask the Court if you can be shown that document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My apologies to the Court. I really have ought to have asked that he be shown document D158.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see on that document near the top the words: "Komanda one Korpus"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see some words written immediately below that. What are those words? What do they mean?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the establishment of the brigade that is one sector that existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the sector that you see there described?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it dealt with morale, psychological problems of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue. Tell us what it does and then I will get back to you. You were saying it dealt with morale, psychological problems. Go on.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Psychological aspects, cultural and entertainment, lectures, cultural evenings. All of those things that in some ways could relax the people in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what I am asking you to do is to tell us exactly what those words say.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sector for morale."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go on. What does it say after that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Psychological, social and military questions."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there the initials or the acronym "IPD"? What is that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sector for morale, conduct, psychological issues, social issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would just respectfully ask the Court to take note of the translation provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But perhaps before doing so, could we ask the witness -- Mr. Hadzic, could you tell us what stands "VP" for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Military questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I just make one aspect of your testimony clear, when, if you recall the month in 1993, did your brigade receive 81-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say precisely, but in late 1993, we received one mortar of 81 millimetres calibre. It is a subcalibre. And this is what we used to train people. We didn't have shells for it. We had to adjust the shells for it in order to use them, and that was the problem with that weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that 81 millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first receive mortars that you could use?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While preparing for assault operations in --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 1994. We received mortars which we were preparing for those combat activities. And we transferred them to the area of responsibility that we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which month, if you can remember, and which year?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1994, in the spring. In the spring of 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in cross-examination that there were police units located in a building behind a school, and you showed us an area to the east of the positions that you controlled. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These police units, can you tell us briefly, what was their function or role?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were located in Dobrinja. We were not very well armed. We didn't have enough people so they had their own area of responsibility. They had their own command and they held that area of responsibility. The part of the territory that they controlled was an area that could be used for the passage of tanks and they also had anti-armour weapons. So this is why they were responsible for that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they armed with infantry weapons, like rifles as well?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They only had infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that there was no sniper nest or you were not aware of a sniper nest in the school in Dobrinja. Could you tell us what do you mean or what -- when you speak of a "sniper," what are you speaking of when you respond to these questions? What do you mean when you were using the word, "sniper"?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify a little bit what you are asking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You answered quite a few questions about whether there were or were not snipers or sniper nests at a school on the eastern frontier of your area of responsibility. I just want to know, what do you mean when you use or you answer a question to the expression or word, "sniper"? What do you mean by "sniper"?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, a sniper is a trained, educated person with special weapons. It is a special kind of person that can carry out that kind of a dirty job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the police units or your units in that area trained in that way?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units of the 5th Motorised were not trained in that way. These were people who received only superficial training. They were just people -- normal, regular people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were shown a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may have a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were shown a document written by one Stjepan Siber and you said he was a part of the headquarters of the army. Do you know what ethnicity he was? From which ethnic group he was from?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was suggested to you, when you were shown a passage from that document that the 5th Dobrinja Brigade were being accused of shooting. I would like you to have a look at that document, with the leave of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is document D164.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you look at that document in your own language and tell me if there is any part, particularly that part of it dealing with the 15th of July 1992, from page 107 and page 108, can you tell us if it says in that entry anything about a complaint being made about persons or any UNPROFOR soldier who was shot from Dobrinja -- I beg your pardon, was shot from areas controlled by the 5th Motorised Brigade? Do you see that there? Could you have a look at it and let me know.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document -- or the date referred to is the 15th of July, which is 9 or 10 days after the official formation of the 5th Motorised Brigade. On or around the 15th of July, 1992, was the 5th Motorised Brigade in full control of all the armed forces in the Dobrinja area?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of July, I stated yesterday that we needed two months in order to complete the establishment of the brigade. We had problems in digging trenches, callup, looking for locations, food supplies, all of those things which were necessary for it to be able to exist. But I would also like to say that at that point we did not control the entire area of the Dobrinja. And it was possible from three or four places in Dobrinja that we did not control, to have sniper fire come from those areas and accuse us of doing it because we had Dobrinja III and Dobrinja IV, which had a view of Dobrinja I and Dobrinja II, and they were covering the Airport Settlement as well as the area around the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at document 163.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With the leave of the Court, can he be handed document 163.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Quickly, in respect to my last question, nine days after the brigade was officially organised, that is the 15th of July 1992, did you have full control of all the Bosnian forces in Dobrinja at that time? It would be helpful if you could tell me.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at document 163. You were asked or it was suggested to you in respect to that document that there was fire coming from your area of control. Could you look at that document and tell me whether or not it states or suggests any allegation that fire was coming from any area controlled by the 5th Motorised Brigade in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. As far as I can see, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever been charged with a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is the cross-examination, Mr. President. There is one area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Re-examination, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Re-examination. There is one area which does not arise directly from the cross-examination, with perhaps the leave of the Court I could ask the leave of the Court to clarify, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are strict on the Defence and we are also strict, it would be of vital importance, whether it is just one of the issues you have forgotten, then there will be no opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think if we had clear answers on something which the answer is possibly there but may require an inference, if the witness could give us a clear answer to the question I am asking, it could be of some assistance to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that be a question that has been put to him at an earlier occasion --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From my review of the records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is not really vital --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is vital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may put the question to the witness. We will then decide whether it is vital, after we have heard Mr. Piletta-Zanin, and we will then see whether the witness can answer the question. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know what is the question the Prosecution would like to ask, but perhaps they could state it clearly so that we can follow them for once and then perhaps the witness could leave the courtroom, the Prosecution could tell us their point of view, and then maybe we can then take the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it is better done not in the presence of the witness. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom just for a very short moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which question would it be, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness said yesterday that the area on the map which he drew between the entrance of the tunnel and the buildings in Dobrinja that is a trench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He said that on the 12th of July, 1993, there was just a meadow there. I just wish to clarify with him, when exactly that communication trench between the entrance of the tunnel and the buildings were built.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may put that question to the witness, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Therefore, the consequence being is that if there is need, we could re-intervene?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can tell you why, if you want the reason. That question was on my list of questions as well. So it is for that extent it is just a matter of who puts the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Mr. President, if this question had been on His Honour's list, after you would have asked it, then I would have been able to intervene, following the rule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if a new element comes up, then, of course it always has been allowed the Defence. That goes even without saying. Please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could he be shown Exhibit P3732. And could it be put on the ELMO so we can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The ELMO is not of great assistance at this very moment. Yes, now it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to look at and point to the part of the red line where you said there was a communication trench between the buildings of the Dobrinja and the entrance to the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that communication trench was constructed?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right after the tunnel was opened. That's when the communication trench was started from the house next to the tunnel because it turned out that people going into that building were creating a crowd and it was possible to see them from Gavrica Brdo, so then for the sake of security, a trench was dug from that house up to the entrance of the tunnel here, so that people would be safer. And they were less noticeable from the Gavrica hill, if they use the trench.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said "right after the tunnel was opened." Is it possible for you to be a little bit more precise. Can you tell us what do you mean by "right after". How soon after? I understand you may have to approximate.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The work on the tunnel was continuous, so from the 30th of July, in that period up until September, that's when that was carried out. Because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I am asking you to do you said the construction of this trench began right after the 30th of July. What do you mean by "right after"? How long after the 30th of July did you begin to dig that or construct that trench?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It started about 10 days after the 30th of July. I can't be sure exactly, but that is my estimate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You may take that away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you had one question. You asked for one clarification, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. First of all, I think that we should clarify for the transcript on this issue, and I would like to re-intervene with your leave, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, first, ask whether the Judges have any questions, so that you can add all the questions at one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions to you. Questioned by the Court

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I need the help of Mr. Usher with the Exhibit 3732 the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes, please put that on the ELMO. I think that you marked the spots of the various shelling incidents except one which is the incident of the 22nd of January 1994 in Alipasino Polje. May I take it that Alipasino Polje is not shown on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Is not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I have a question on that. The first one is that whether you went to Alipasino Polje during the war, let's say, until September 1994?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just passing through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: But you went there, you passed through Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I was passing through to the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: The second question is: How far is Alipasino Polje from Dobrinja? Let's say from the building of the brigade headquarters, as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 2 and 3.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: All right. That is enough. Can we see in this map the Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see the Orthodox church on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: The Faculty of Theology?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you can't see that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since Judge El Mahdi has some more questions for you and I have some more questions for you as well, perhaps we first take the break. We will adjourn until 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] I would like to ask you if you can inform me about the scale of the map which is in front of you, approximately, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer. Perhaps 1 to 1.000, something like that, I don't know,. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Approximately.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1 to 10.000. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe that you know, according to your military experience that the field of firing of a rifle, of a gun which was used by the former JNA for the snipers, do you know the range, the firing range of a rifle, of a sniping rifle?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1500 to 1800 metres. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So it is not possible that that would go over one kilometre, 1.8 kilometres, in your opinion, it wouldn't go over that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you. You indicated on the map the headquarters of the brigade called the Dobrinja Brigade and you said that the headquarters of the brigade was located in a building which had eight floors. Did I understand you correctly? Is that true? Is that how I should have understood it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Six or eight floors. I cannot be absolutely certain, but it was a higher building. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, but if I understand you correctly, your headquarters was located on the first floor and it was from the second floor, until the sixth or the eighth floor were these floors occupied by civilians, did civilians live on the second to the eighth floor?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command was not on the first floor. It was in the cellar of that building, in the basement of that building. And it used business premises above the basement of that building. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. So one could say that the command was in the basement but that there were soldiers who were on the first or on the second floor, and apart from that, the other floors were civilians located on other floors?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first and second floor, there were no military -- there were no troops there. If the apartments were not destroyed vertically, then civilians did inhabit those apartment. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But there were civilians living there during the period of -- from 1992 to 1994, there were civilians living there?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And is this also valid for other headquarters of battalions, of battalions of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Battalion commands were located in those buildings because we did not have any other choice. These were commands which were practically unarmed in those parts of buildings. There were no military facilities there so that we could locate our command somewhere where there would be no civilians living there. The only possible possibility that we had for the armed formations for the Dobrinja Brigade to locate them for the companies and the platoons, we kept them in the area of responsibility, in the trenches and the buildings that had been abandoned. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you. You said, and I am quoting: [In English] "Forming the line of defence." [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, these were buildings that were destroyed or semi-destroyed and you were using them as means of defence. Did I understand you correctly? Is this what you said?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were destroyed and abandoned buildings. There were no civilians living there. These were destroyed and abandoned buildings. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But before they were destroyed, they had been inhabited by civilians, these had been civilian buildings, residential buildings where civilians had lived. Did the headquarters change or move during the period of the conflict, the location, the location of the headquarters, did they change?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Battalion commands, no. Command of brigades changed three or four times. They moved to the neighbouring building and then they moved back, changed location within the building. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Was this in order to avoid the firing from the opposing side? This was for military purposes that they changed?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say for military purposes. For security purposes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] For security purposes. You mean for military security. Could you perhaps clarify? This is so that they would not be targeted by the opposing side?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was in the way that the change of the location would protect. What we were worried about that if we stayed in the location too long, that this information would reach the opposing side about where we were and then somebody from the command would get killed, which is the reason why we changed the location. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. In relation to the tunnel, you said that the tunnel was operational from the end of July 1992. And when did the work on the tunnel begin?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: End of July 1993. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was March 1993 that the work on the tunnel had begun. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And you said that people would then usually get together or were grouped in a building which was in front of the trenches. The workers, you explained it well, but there were soldiers who took part in the construction work of the tunnel. So were there also civilians who took part in this work?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] As a soldier, one would imagine that women had also taken part in military work. Were there also women who were taking part in the construction work?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among the people from our brigade, there was not a single woman who had taken part in the construction of the tunnel. Because the whole procedure of digging the tunnel had been dealt with by logistics of the 1st Corps and we had to provide people to dig every seven days, and people went in shifts in order to dig the tunnel. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And during the work, was this location targeted by the opposing side? You said that the opposing side was not aware of the entrance to the tunnel. Is that true, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the work and the digging, there was no particularly heavy firing on our side of the location where the tunnel had been -- the digging had been ongoing. So there were shells landing of equal intensity. It wasn't -- after the tunnel had been dug, the second part of the tunnel was more intensely belt, it was probably that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had seen and then they started to shell more intensely, our side. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, but if I understood you correctly, they did not know exactly where the entrance to the tunnel was.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my personal feeling. I think they did not know where the entrance to the tunnel was. And on these locations when the tunnel was fully operational, there were occasionally 2 or 3.000 people who couldn't all fit into the surrounding building that were right close in the vicinity of the tunnel. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And these people, where were they? Where was their accommodation? You said that they were not in the nearby buildings. Were they in the buildings near, but were they in the area of the -- near the area of the entrance to the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried to move these people who were waiting to go into the tunnel, to move them because of the shelling, but there were so many people at times that we couldn't move them and they still waited in front of the tunnel and near the building which was near to the entrance to the tunnel. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I have a few questions for you as well. You told us that at the beginning of the conflict quite number of people were pressed to leave Dobrinja, but that many had remained there. Has it ever been considered to evacuate further parts of the population?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any movement represented a danger for us, any movement of the population in Dobrinja. We had plans in the event of a breakthrough of the lines, in case the enemy troops entered Dobrinja, then we would, with the assistance of the civil protection, enable the population to leave Dobrinja. But in any case, any movement of our population presented a danger for the survival of Dobrinja because if a man that you had, if you allowed his family to leave, then he wasn't much more use to you any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain that last part of your answer?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were afraid that if we evacuated, for no reason, if we evacuated the people to the city without any reason, then very quickly the soldiers whose families were evacuated would leave Dobrinja. Because the psychological pressure of how the families are, how they were living, how they were getting on, would have an effect on those people, and then it would perhaps make it easier for them or make it possible for them to go, to leave the brigade and go to be with their families, if something like this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever consider that the presence of civilians in Dobrinja perhaps would prevent a, I would say, an attack that would destroy the whole area, and therefore the presence of civilians would, to that extent, partially protect Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question is: It was not quite clear to me what your answer was on the question of the intensity of the shelling of the buildings where the headquarters were located. Was that similar to whatever other buildings or did you receive more fire at the buildings where your headquarters were located, either a battalion or the brigade headquarter?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not more or less than the rest of Dobrinja. So, the battalion commands and the brigade commands were not exposed to more intense shelling than the other parts of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you ever considered to evacuate the civilians from the buildings where the headquarters were located, so not evacuation on a large scale, but just from the buildings where the headquarters were located in the "sous-sol," as they say it in French.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two buildings where the commands were situated, the command of the 1st Battalion and the brigade command there was a very large atomic shelter. So we would bring the civilians from -- in from the edges of Dobrinja where they were living to shield them from artillery fire or from combat. So we tried to protect them from that. And we tried to bring them into the central parts of Dobrinja. And then after a while, we didn't have any more maneuvering space because about 3.000 apartments were completely demolished in Dobrinja and another 2000 which would not -- which were not habitable. So the zone where we were in, it was very difficult. It wasn't of much use for the civilians. The concentration of people was highest in the central parts of the settlement, while the buildings in the central part of the settlement are very large buildings with four or five entrances, with six, seven, or eight floors, with three to four apartments per floor, so one staircase from top to bottom would have 24 apartments. So, if in that building, one vertical line was destroyed, then you had to find other 24 apartments somewhere else or put two or more families in one apartment. So this was physically impossible because there simply wasn't enough space.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My last question is: Looking at the map and listening to your answer as far as the scale of this map, approximately, is concerned, would it be correct to say that the distance from the nearest building to the entrance of the tunnel would be approximately 150 metres or?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About that much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About 150 metres?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, I have two observations to make. The first one is that I have the impression, I have to say it now, that one of the questions of His Honour Mr. El Mahdi was not reported in the transcript and this is 38.39. I believe that the witness did answer, but this did not come out into the transcript. I don't know whether this is correct. Perhaps we can have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said 38.39. You are referring to pages, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Pages 38, line 8, line 9. [Interpretation] Eight and nine. We can see that two questions of His Honour Mr. El Mahdi come after one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree that two questions come after each other. I have -- it is not in my recollection whether there was any answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness had said yes to the first of the questions. And I apologise. I did not want to interrupt His Honour, Judge El Mahdi, but I think that it would be good to intervene now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is not in my recollection any more. So we will have to check that at the -- at the audio tape, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could ask the witness. A question has been put to you by Judge El Mahdi saying that "but before they were destroyed," and he was talking about buildings, destroyed and abandoned buildings, "they had been inhabited by civilians, these had been civilian buildings, residential buildings where civilians had lived." You answered in the affirmative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is then clear for the transcript. Please proceed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have three questions to ask. Thank you. But before that, Mr. President, it would be good to consider that after the witness can tell us what happened to the famous line between the trench and the tunnel on the screen, on the ELMO, this was not reported in the transcript. It would be good if we can explain it for the transcript with the help of the usher. If it can be put again on the ELMO, which is already the case. Thank you. And clarify the situation. Further cross-examination by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in relation to the tunnel line, I can see two points on this map, one which corresponds to a red circle and the other one which corresponds to a red dot. Is it true that the red dot corresponds to the entrance of the tunnel which was dug under a house, yes or no, and perhaps if you can indicate the dot on the map so that we can all have it clear.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that is not what I mean. I meant the other dot, further up.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that one.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the communication road Kasindolska Street-Kula. Below the road or the communication, there was a small tunnel which was dug between the front and the back trench.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you had started the work in digging under a house. Is that the house that we can see to the right of the red dot?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just in order to prevent whatever confusion. When the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Answered yes, he pointed at the red circle, not at the red dot. Where I had the impression that when you were talking about "under a house" that you are rather referring to the red dot, than to the red circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I saw him indicate the red dot. Perhaps he could be given a different pointer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He now again points to the small circle and that is what I saw him doing before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you started the work under a house. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please indicate where is the house under which you had started the work?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, where do you see a sign of a house, symbol for a house on this map?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see houses around here. This was a settlement. This was a settlement here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you agree with me if I said that around the red circle there are no houses?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, there are no houses? The tunnel -- we started to dig under a house. You can still see that house today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So I will go on with other questions. Witness, could you tell us when did you start the work on the trenches, not necessarily the tunnel, but the trenches?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On which trenches do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are talking about the trenches linking supposedly the entrance to the tunnel and Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago, about 10 days after the opening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You said that 2 to 3.000 people would gather near the tunnel. Where would they gather, could you please indicate for us on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this building where there was the definitive entrance to the tunnel, this building which was completely destroyed, and nobody lived there, from the buildings below in the garages of these houses, people would shelter and wait those people who waited and those who couldn't find any accommodation, they were waiting outside, near the tunnel, in the area near the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, Mr. President, the witness indicated two buildings which were to the north of the vertical red line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if it was necessary to have an authorisation for the civilians who were going to use the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every civilian had to have permission. If they were able-bodied or not, they had to have permission from the Ministry of Defence, or if they were unable to do military service, to have a certificate and to have a permission, if they are civilians, from the Ministry of the Interior and also a permission to go through the tunnel. And this was used by the civilian authorities, to these people who were not members of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
